definition: Extant means still existing, not destroyed or lost.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Of the balloon photographs taken over the city in 1906, eleven are extant, and nine of those show the same church.

Attested is a weaker claim than extant — a lost symphony known only from the printed program of its premiere is attested, nothing more; an extant work, however scorched or stained, still physically exists.
Intact goes further than extant: an extant manuscript may be a single scorched leaf, while an intact one has come through whole.

Surviving is the everyday word for what has come through when much around it was lost, and it fits people as naturally as papers. Extant is the scholar's ledger word for things — editions, specimens, recordings — that time has not yet destroyed, said when counting what remains.

Existing just means in being right now, with no story attached — existing rules, existing buildings. Extant carries the drama of the count: said of things time usually eats, it quietly reports that this particular one has not been destroyed or lost along the way.

Yet four cylinders are extant — two with collectors in Melbourne, one in a university basement, one found wedged inside a player sold at a farm auction.

Extant means still existing, not destroyed or lost, and it is said precisely of things time usually eats.
Note what the word does not claim: condition.
An extant cylinder may be cracked past playing — extant reports only that the thing itself has not vanished from the world.
Extant is catalog language — editions, specimens, recordings, buildings — and it often follows its noun ("three copies are extant").

Use surviving in ordinary prose; reach for extant when counting what time has spared, and note the contrast baked into its antonym: a species is extinct, but the two museum skins of it are, strangely, still extant.

Film historians estimate that seven in ten American silent features are gone -- burned in vault fires, melted down for their silver, or simply thrown away.
Against that arithmetic, the archive's new catalogue reads like a rescue log.
For each title it records one word where it matters most: extant.
The entry does not promise beauty.
An extant film may be one reel of five, water-spotted, missing its ending.
It promises something narrower and better: the thing itself still physically exists, somewhere, on a shelf a researcher can visit.
Titles known only from posters and newspaper advertisements get a different, sadder label, and a separate list.
